rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most scholars place al-Fātiḥah among the earliest sūrahs revealed in Makkah.
rows.anchor: to have been revealed in Makkah

rows.speaker: Mujāhid
rows.claim: Mujāhid says al-Fātiḥah was revealed in Madinah.
rows.anchor: According to Mujāhid (d. 104/722–23), one of the leading scholars among the second generation of Muslims, this sūrah was revealed in Madinah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most scholars reject a Medinan origin because Muslims needed the sūrah to perform obligatory prayers.
rows.anchor: Most scholars claim that this is impossible, however, as the Muslims would not have been able to perform their required prayers without it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Fātiḥah means The Opening: it opens the Book, each prayer cycle, many everyday acts, and may open the breast to faith.
rows.anchor: The primary meaning of al-Fātiḥah is “The Opening,” which indicates the sūrah’s function as “the opening of the Book”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah is seen as a synthesis and the Quran’s most important chapter, hence Umm al-kitāb; the title also refers to 3:7 and the celestial archetype of scripture.
rows.anchor: has been given the title Umm al-kitāb, “Mother of the Book,” a

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is called the Mother of the Quran because it contains the meaning of the entire Quran.
rows.anchor: It is also known as “The Mother of the Quran” (IK, Ṭ), a reference to its containing the meaning of the entire Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another title, The Seven Oft-Repeated, is linked to 15:87.
rows.anchor: Other titles are “The Seven Oft-Repeated”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The title The Cure reflects its reputed healing power for body and soul.
rows.anchor: is said to have healing powers for both body and soul

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The title The Foundation reflects the Fātiḥah’s role as a foundation for the whole Quran.
rows.anchor: because it serves as a foundation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As Sūrat al-Ḥamd and Sūrat al-Ṣalāh, the Fātiḥah begins each prayer cycle for Sunnis and many Shiites.
rows.anchor: the Fātiḥah is recited at the beginning of each

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shiite law permits reciting the Fātiḥah in the third and fourth cycles or an alternative formula praising God.
rows.anchor: In Shiite law one is allowed to recite the Fātiḥah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims recite the Fātiḥah at diverse life events; funeral services are called fātiḥah in some lands as an opening from one life to another.
rows.anchor: It is also recited by Muslims on occasions as diverse as a funeral, a wedding, the birth of a child, the inauguration of an official event

rows.speaker: Prophet Muhammad
rows.claim: The Prophet identifies the Fātiḥah as the greatest sūrah, calling it Praise be to God and the seven oft-repeated, and linking it to 15:87.
rows.anchor: the Prophet told a man that he would teach him the greatest sūrah; when asked what it was, the Prophet responded

rows.speaker: God
rows.claim: In a hadith qudsī, God responds to the servant’s praise, magnification, and glorification during the prayer, which is divided between them.
rows.anchor: I have divided the prayer between Myself and My

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Fātiḥah is a prayer encapsulating metaphysical and eschatological realities and teaches the proper human disposition toward God.
rows.anchor: the Fātiḥah is more than the confessional prayer of Muslims. It is a prayer that encapsulates all the metaphysical and eschatological realities

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Its structure moves from God’s nature in the first three verses, through the God-human relationship, to human states in the final three.
rows.anchor: The Fātiḥah thus has a threefold structure: the first three verses deal with the nature of God, the middle verse deals with the relationship between God and human beings

rows.speaker: Prophet Muhammad
rows.claim: A report says nothing like the Fātiḥah was revealed in the Torah, Psalms, Gospel, or Quran.
rows.anchor: In one the Prophet says, “By Him in Whose Hand lies my soul, in neither the Torah, the Psalms, the Gospel, nor the Quran was the like of it revealed”

rows.speaker: Mujāhid
rows.claim: One attribution says Satan was frightened when the Fātiḥah was revealed, among four events; others attribute the saying to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: attributed by some to Mujāhid (Q) and by

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Fātiḥah’s exalted status generated many independent commentaries, often showing how the Quran as a whole is contained in it.
rows.anchor: The exalted status of the Fātiḥah has resulted in numerous independent commentaries upon it, some numbering hundreds of pages

rows.speaker: ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib
rows.claim: A saying attributed to ʿAlī compresses the Quran into the Fātiḥah, the basmalah, its opening bāʾ, and the diacritical point beneath it.
rows.anchor: a famous saying attributed to ʿAlī ibn AbīṬālib

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The point beneath bāʾ can symbolize the Divine Pen’s first drop of ink, which inscribed all archetypes on the Preserved Tablet before creation; thus basmalah marks both Quranic and cosmic beginnings.
rows.anchor:
This point can be understood to represent the first
drop of ink

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every sūrah except one opens with the basmalah, also found in 27:30.
rows.anchor: known as the basmalah in Arabic

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Scholars disagree whether the basmalah is a verse of each sūrah or a marker beginning a new sūrah.
rows.anchor: There is a debate as to whether the basmalah is a verse of each sūrah or an indication of the beginning of a new sūrah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Except in Shāfiʿī and Jaʿfarī law, most schools do not recite the basmalah with sūrahs during daily prayers.
rows.anchor: with the exception of the Shāfiʿī and Jaʿfarī schools

rows.speaker: Anas ibn Mālik
rows.claim: Anas reports that the Prophet and first three caliphs began prayer recitation with Praise be to God, omitting the basmalah.
rows.anchor: Anas ibn Mālik (d. 91/709), a close Companion of the Prophet, is reported to have said, “I have prayed behind the Prophet, Abū Bakr

rows.speaker: Abū Hurayrah
rows.claim: Abū Hurayrah recited the basmalah while leading prayer and said his prayer most resembled the Messenger’s.
rows.anchor: Abū Hurayrah (d. 61/681), another of the Prophet’s Companions, is reported to have recited the basmalah

rows.speaker: Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq
rows.claim: Jaʿfar calls the basmalah the greatest Quranic verse; Shiite scholars consequently treat it as a verse of the Fātiḥah and every sūrah beginning with it.
rows.anchor: Based upon a saying of Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq (d. 148/765), the sixth Shiite Imam

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some scholars count the basmalah as a verse separate from the sūrahs that begin with it.
rows.anchor: Others say that it is a verse, though separate from the

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAbbās
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that revelation of the basmalah taught the Prophet where one sūrah ends and the next begins.
rows.anchor: Ibn ʿAbbās (d. 68/687), a cousin of the Prophet who was among the most important scholars of the Quran in the first generation of Muslims

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The basmalah, or its shortened form, consecrates licit actions because all things should be done for God’s sake and in His Name.
rows.anchor: The basmalah, or its shortened form, In the Name of God, is employed by pious Muslims to consecrate all licit actions

rows.speaker: Prophet Muhammad
rows.claim: The Prophet says an important matter not begun in God’s Name will be cut off.
rows.anchor: the Prophet said, “Any important matter not begun with the Name of God shall be cut off”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition bi may govern an implied verb such as begin or seek help, or a noun, with the phrase either preceding or following it.
rows.anchor: could imply a verb at the beginning of the sentence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation makes God’s opening in His Name an invitation for people to begin, unite, and commence through His Name as well.
rows.anchor: so you too begin,” as if God were saying

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some consider Allāh a unique word without a root; others derive it from al-Ilāh, meaning the Divine.
rows.anchor: God renders Allāh, which according to some is a unique word with no root and according to others derives from the word al-Ilāh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran shows pre-Islamic Arabs knew the name Allāh as creator, although most idol worshippers denied His supreme sovereignty in the Age of Ignorance.
rows.anchor: The Quranic usage of Allāh indicates that it was already known to the pre-Islamic Arabs, as in 43:87

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Allāh is the most universal and all-embracing Divine Name, yet uniquely applies only to God, unlike other Divine Names.
rows.anchor: Allāh is not only the most universal and all-embracing Name, but also the most specific of the Divine Names

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some call Allāh the All-Encompassing Name, comprising all divine Names and Attributes.
rows.anchor: Some referto Allāh as the All-Encompassing Name

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The order Allāh, al-Raḥmān, al-Raḥīm can symbolize Essence, unity of Attributes, and unity of divine acts, respectively.
rows.anchor: The ordering of the three Divine Names in the basmalah can be seen as an allusion to the levels of Divinity in relation to the created order

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ḥamd praises God for His qualities and thanks Him for worldly favors and next-world reward.
rows.anchor: Praise translates al-ḥamd, which indicates extolling the Praiseworthy

rows.speaker: Prophet Muhammad
rows.claim: The Prophet says that praising God, Lord of the worlds, constitutes thanks and brings increased bounty.
rows.anchor: the Prophet is reported to have said, “When you say, ‘Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds,’ you will have thanked God and He will increase your bounty”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thanks responds to what has already been received, while praise is more universal because it extols qualities prior to any gift.
rows.anchor: is given for what one has already received

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The definite form al-ḥamd indicates that all praise and gratitude belong to God.
rows.anchor: is rendered in the definite rather than the indefinite to indicate

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God praises Himself in the opening so humans can praise Him in divine speech, which He knows is more adequate than their own words.
rows.anchor: It is said that God has praised Himself in this opening address so that human beings can praise God in the speech of God

rows.speaker: Prophet Muhammad
rows.claim: The Prophet acknowledges that no one can enumerate praise due to God, who is as He praised Himself.
rows.anchor: the Prophet is reported to have addressed God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims use the basmalah to consecrate actions at their beginning and al-ḥamd to thank God upon completion; etiquette answers any inquiry about one’s condition with praise.
rows.anchor: whereas the basmalah is employed to consecrate a deed at its beginning, Praise be to God is employed to thank God for an act or event upon its completion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rabb denotes master, arranger, and possessor; of God it means peerless Master who orders affairs and owns creation.
rows.anchor: Lord renders rabb, which refers to a master

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some relate rabb to cultivation: God is caretaker and trainer of things and of human souls, hearts, and spirits.
rows.anchor: since God is the Caretaker

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some take the worlds as four communities: humans, jinn, angels, and satans.
rows.anchor: Some say it refers to four communities: human beings, jinn, angels, and satans

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Others restrict the worlds to humans and jinn because only these communities need a warner, as in 25:1.
rows.anchor: others say it refers only to human beings and jinn, since the Prophet is referred to as a warner unto the worlds (25:1)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other interpretations include human generations, every species, or all levels from earth through the seven heavens.
rows.anchor: It may also refer to the different generations of human beings, to all of the species in creation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say the worlds are all existent things other than God; al-Rāzī adds that God can actualize infinitely many unknown universes, making Him Lord of all existence and space.
rows.anchor: Thus some say that in the most universal sense the worlds refers to all existent things other than God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm repeat the basmalah’s names in every sūrah except al-Tawbah, and intensify the meaning of mercy.
rows.anchor: Both Names are intensifications of the word raḥmah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Raḥmān is considered more emphatic and encompassing than al-Raḥīm; it uniquely names God’s mercy that brings existence, while al-Raḥīm concerns sustaining nourishment and can describe creatures, including the Prophet.
rows.anchor: Al-Raḥmān, which is also the title of Sūrah 55, is considered to be more emphatic, embracing, and encompassing than al-Raḥīm

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their relation can be pictured as sunlight over the whole sky and a ray touching an individual creature; 17:110 associates the Compassionate with God’s beautiful Names.
rows.anchor: al-Raḥmān is like the light of the sun that illuminates the whole sky, and al-Raḥīm is like the particular ray of sunlight that touches a creature

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Islamic metaphysics, God’s Breath of the Compassionate upon immutable archetypes brings the world into being, so the world’s existence is the breath of divine compassion.
rows.anchor: the very existence of the world is in essence nothing but the breath

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two Names express universal essential mercy that brings creation forth and particular attributive mercy bestowed on chosen beings, including believers (33:43).
rows.anchor: Together these two Names refer to two aspects of the Divine Mercy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Universal mercy is associated with the Compassionate enthroned (20:5; 25:59); particular mercy sustains each creature differently.
rows.anchor: The essential and universal Mercy is that of the Compassionate, which God bestows upon all things through their very existence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mercy manifests in names of beauty and is veiled in names of rigor by the inseparability of kindness from majesty and divine determining power; God is compassionate to all and merciful to believers.
rows.anchor: God is thus said to be Compassionate toward all of creation and Merciful toward the believers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Placed between God’s sovereignty over space and mastery of time, this verse presents mercy as encompassing all time and space, as in 7:156.
rows.anchor: this verse indicates that God’s Mercy encompasses and interpenetrates all time and all space, as in 7:156

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mālik means master or owner, while malik means king; both readings are traced to the Prophet, with disagreement about which is more comprehensive.
rows.anchor: It is also sometimes read malik, meaning “king” or “sovereign,” and both variants can be traced to the Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say king is more intensive because every king is a master but not every master a king; others say king better expresses God’s disposal over all things.
rows.anchor: Malik (“king”) is understood to be more intensive than mālik (“master”), since every king is a master, but not every master is a king

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God alone rules the Day of Judgment, when all contenders’ claims to sovereignty collapse, as 40:16 declares.
rows.anchor: That God is Master of the Day of Judgment indicates that He alone has sovereignty over the Day of Reckoning

rows.speaker: Prophet Muhammad
rows.claim: The Prophet says God will seize earth, fold the sky with His right hand, and proclaim Himself King over earthly kings and tyrants on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: the Prophet is reported to have said

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Day of Judgment is when the account of jinn and humans comes due and all return to meet God.
rows.anchor: The Day of Judgment is the day on which the account of jinn and human beings comes due

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dīn can denote obedience, custom, way, or affair, although it is most often translated religion.
rows.anchor: Judgment renders dīn, which is etymologically related

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dīn is related to dayn, debt: dīn is repayment of the debt owed to God, who is al-Dayyān, the One Who Repays.
rows.anchor: While dayn refers to a debt, dīn refers to the repayment of our debt to God, and God is also known as al-Dayyān

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Day of dīn is requital and reckoning for worldly deeds, with every soul repaid for its earnings and deeds weighed (24:25; 40:17; 7:8–9).
rows.anchor: The Day of dīn can thus be understood as the day of the requital and reckoning for actions performed in this world

rows.speaker: Prophet Muhammad
rows.claim: The Prophet calls believers most intelligent when they often remember death and prepare well for what follows.
rows.anchor: the Prophet replied, “The most frequent

rows.speaker: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb
rows.claim: ʿUmar urges people to take account of themselves and weigh their deeds before the final accounting.
rows.anchor: Following upon the Prophet’s advice, the second Caliph, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sequence of divine Names descends from Essence through universal and particular mercy to divine management of creation; the Fātiḥah’s second half then ascends back toward the Principle.
rows.anchor: the progression of Names in vv. 1–4 reflects the descent of the created order from the Divine Principle. The second half of the Fātiḥah then pertains to the ascent

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 5 shifts from describing God to direct second-person address; the first-person plural represents people and creation, expressing humility before God.
rows.anchor: In v. 5 begins the direct address of God in the second person, a marked change from the praise and description of God in vv. 1–4

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naʿbudu means worship, servitude, obedience, and adoration; the verse acknowledges all creation as God’s servants and places the direct object before the verb to express complete servitude.
rows.anchor: We worship renders the verb naʿbudu, which also indicates servitude, obedience, and adoration

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Direct second-person address establishes an I-Thou relation and gives every person access to God without a priestly intermediary; worshippers should be fully present and devote religion solely to Him.
rows.anchor: Addressing God in the second person rather than the third person indicates a direct I-Thou relationship

rows.speaker: Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq
rows.claim: Jaʿfar distinguishes worship from fear, for reward, and from love; worship out of love is free worship and most excellent.
rows.anchor: Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq is reported to have said

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some define true servitude as maximal humility and self-effacement; it acknowledges human poverty and reliance on God (47:38).
rows.anchor: the greatest degree of humility and self-effacement before God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Servitude precedes seeking help because one first recognizes the sovereign’s power; help is requested for worship and all affairs, since people never act independently or worship by their own strength.
rows.anchor: The expression of servitude necessarily precedes the statement that one “seeks help” from God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After asking for help in obedience, the worshipper asks for perseverance and firmness in truth, as God guides believers through faith (10:9).
rows.anchor: guide us can be understood as a prayer for perseverance in following the straight path and thus for continued aid

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Guidance can mean desire for intimacy, nearness, knowledge, and love of God; mystics paraphrase it as directing hearts and aspirations toward Him and from Him.
rows.anchor: The request for guidance also implies seeking to be led to God Himself and thus a desire for intimacy with Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Intellectually, the straight path means using God-given intelligence correctly to reach truth instead of reasoning toward error.
rows.anchor: following the straight path can be understood to mean using one’s God-given intelligence correctly in order to reach the truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The straight path is a clear, uncurved road; religiously it is a middle way joining outward Law and inward spirituality, with outer servitude and inner freedom.
rows.anchor: From a religious perspective, it is a middle way that avoids worldliness, on the one hand, and extreme asceticism, on the other

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet guides his community on this path; the Muslim community is a middle community in all dimensions of life.
rows.anchor: middle community (2:143) that follows a middle way in action

rows.speaker: Prophet Muhammad
rows.claim: A prophetic parable identifies the path as Islam, its walls as God’s limits, doors as prohibitions, the gate-caller as the Book, and the caller above as divine admonition in the heart.
rows.anchor: The straight path is Islam, the two walls are the limits set by God, while the doors refer to what God has prohibited

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Commentators identify the path with the Quran, Islam, or the Prophet; Shiite readings identify ʿAlī or the Prophet and Imams, while Sunni accounts name the Prophet and Abū Bakr and ʿUmar.
rows.anchor: Some see the straight path as a reference to the Quran itself (Ṭ, Ṭū, Ṭs), while others say that it refers to Islam

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The path can mean walking with God toward God: God guides believers to Himself (4:175), while God Himself is on a straight path (11:56).
rows.anchor: To be on the straight path, or a straight path as it is usually presented in the Quran, can also be understood as walking with God to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The straight path is also interpreted as the post-Judgment traverse across which beings pass at varying speeds, with some falling into Hellfire.
rows.anchor: The straight path is also understood as a reference to the traverse that human beings and jinn must cross as the final stage of Judgment

rows.speaker: Prophet Muhammad
rows.claim: The Prophet describes the traverse as finer than a hair and sharper than a sword, crossed at varying speeds or ending in a fall to Hell.
rows.anchor: According to the Prophet, this traverse is “finer than a hair and sharper than a sword”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some accounts divide the final verse into two verses, with the first ending at hast blessed.
rows.anchor: According to some accounts, this verse is in fact two verses, the first of which ends with hast blessed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those God blessed are identified in 4:69 as prophets, truthful ones, witnesses, and righteous people, excellent companions.
rows.anchor: Whosoever obeys God and the Messenger, they are with those whom God has blessed, the prophets, the truthful ones, the witnesses, and the righteous

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The blessed are also described as purified for attaining God or as observing the Law while realizing spiritual truths without exceeding knowledge or its decrees.
rows.anchor: Those who are blessed by God are also said to be those whom God has purified, so that they are able to attain unto Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghayr may attach grammatically to the path or to those, but both readings yield the same meaning.
rows.anchor: Not of renders the exceptive particle ghayr, which is understood as being attached to the path

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some commentators identify those incurring wrath with idolaters and those astray with hypocrites.
rows.anchor: According to some, those who incur wrath are the idolaters, and those who are astray are the hypocrites

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation associates disbelief with wrath and lesser sins with straying.
rows.anchor: Others relate the terms to two categories of sin in which disbelief incurs wrath and lesser sin results from being astray

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Others associate the terms with moral shortcomings such as heedlessness and profligacy, broadly encompassing spiritual debasement and worldly preoccupation.
rows.anchor: Still others relate the terms to those who exhibit various moral shortcomings, such as those who are heedless and those who are profligate

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other Quranic passages describe divine wrath against disbelief, disputants, hypocrites, idolaters, and murderers of believers.
rows.anchor: Regarding those who incur wrath, 16:106 says, Whosoever opens his breast unto disbelief, upon them shall be the Wrath of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran frequently describes disbelievers, those who exchange belief for disbelief, and caprice-followers without guidance as astray.
rows.anchor: Regarding those who are astray, a far more prevalent Quranic concept, 3:90 states

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse prays to follow those whom God elevates in belief, knowledge, and uncorrupted faith, and to avoid disbelievers, some astray and some under wrath.
rows.anchor: the final verse of this sūrah can be understood as a prayer (1) to follow the way of those whom God raises in degrees

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 6–7 depict humanity’s journey toward God and request an honorable approach rather than a disgraced one, echoing the image of walking upright on a straight path.
rows.anchor: vv. 6–7 refer to the manner in which all human beings are moving toward their Lord

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Past-tense blessedness conveys completed certainty, while passive wrath leaves room for repentance and avoids attributing injustice to God, who does not wrong people.
rows.anchor: Those whom Thou hast blessed conveys an action performed by God in the past tense, thus giving a sense of finality and certitude

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Straying may be intentional or mistaken; Moses called himself astray before his mission, and God says He found Muhammad astray and guided him, so the term can cover those not living by revelation.
rows.anchor: Being astray can result from something intentional or something done by mistake

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On a vertical ascent reading, wrath represents descent from God and straying represents horizontal wandering; together they symbolize three spatial dimensions and human possibilities.
rows.anchor: those who incur wrath can be understood as a reference to those upon a path of descent away from God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A prophetic saying, not considered highly authentic, identifies those under wrath as Jews and those astray as Christians.
rows.anchor: Based upon a saying attributed to the Prophet, though not considered to be of the highest degree of authenticity

rows.speaker: Prophet Muhammad
rows.claim: A hadith promises forgiveness of past sins when a worshipper’s Āmīn coincides with the angels’ Āmīn.
rows.anchor: According to a ḥadīth, “When the prayer leader says

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sunnis customarily say Āmīn after the Fātiḥah; it is recommended, not obligatory, and scholars differ whether it should be said aloud or quietly.
rows.anchor: Upon the completion of the Fātiḥah, it is thus customary among Sunni Muslims to say Āmīn

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Āmīn is commonly a supplication meaning O God, answer us; others call it a divine Name or say Thus shall it be, akin to Hebrew Amen as an affirmation and seal of prayer.
rows.anchor: Most understand āmīn to mean, “O God! Answer us,” which functions as a supplication

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most commentators attach Most High to Lord, making the verse an injunction to glorify God; attaching it to Name instructs worshippers not to associate other things with God’s Name or to praise Him with revealed Names.
rows.anchor: The Most High can be understood to modify Lord or the Name, though most prefer the former

rows.speaker: Prophet Muhammad
rows.claim: When 56:74 was revealed the Prophet instructed companions to enact it while bowing; for this verse he instructed them to enact it while prostrating.
rows.anchor: when the present verse was revealed, he said, “Enact it when you prostrate”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims recite Glory be to God, the Magnificent three times in bowing and Glory be to God, the Most High three times in prostration.
rows.anchor: Muslims thus say “Glory be to God, the Magnificent” three times when bowing in prayer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Created can refer specifically to humans, to humans and animals, or to all creation.
rows.anchor: Here created refers to human beings in particular, to human beings and animals, or to all of creation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the human-specific reading, God fashioned the first human after breathing His Spirit into him, without irregularity, then measured his form and provided nourishment.
rows.anchor: God fashioned the first human being after breathing into him of His Spirit, leaving him without irregularities

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qaddara can also be read qadara, meaning to have power or determine, so God retains direct power over all He created.
rows.anchor: Measured out renders qaddara, which can also be read qadara, meaning to have power or to determine

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Guidance may be the instinct by which creatures seek their allotted nourishment, or God’s leading people to religion and knowledge of Unity through signs and proofs.
rows.anchor: Here guidance refers to the instinct God puts in all things to be able to seek the nourishment that He has already measured out for them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The broader implication is that creation is properly formed without imperfection or flaw.
rows.anchor: The broader implication is that creation is as it should be, without imperfection or flaw

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pasture and its blackened stubble illustrate God’s power over the creation and destruction of living things; marʿā means all forms of vegetation.
rows.anchor: These verses allude to the manner in which God maintains power over the creation and destruction of all living things
